facts.advisory_summary:
actix-http has HTTP/1.1 CL.TE Request Smuggling  — A vulnerability in `actix-http`'s HTTP/1.1 request parser allows an unauthenticated remote client to smuggle requests in deployments where a front-end HTTP intermediary and the Actix backend disagree about whether `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` defines the request body length.

## Severity

**Medium**.
This is an HTTP request smuggling vulnerability that can be triggered over the network without application-level credentials. Exploitation requires a specific proxy topology: an upstream proxy, WAF, load balancer, or similar in

expect.note: actix-http 3.9.0 is the server for every request (meilisearch main.rs:182-184) HttpServer bind (HTTP/1.1 via HttpService::tcp). The h1 request decoder (actix-http src/h1/decoder.rs:84-205) accepts both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding: chunked, letting chunked win without rejecting the request. It runs on every inbound request, no auth needed. Exploitation needs a front proxy that disagrees on CL/TE; Meilisearch is commonly deployed behind nginx/LB, so treat as reachable. (RustSec function 'awc' is the client, not used, but the advisory is the server parser.)

No call to anyhow::Error::downcast_mut anywhere: grep over crates/ finds only std Any downcast_ref on panic payloads (index-scheduler/src/scheduler/mod.rs:194, process_batch.rs:330) and Box<dyn Any>::downcast (meilisearch/src/analytics/segment_analytics.rs:87); no downcast_mut in anyhow's runtime dependents (lindera-*, tiktoken-rs) either.

facts.advisory_summary:
bytes has integer overflow in BytesMut::reserve — # Details

In the unique reclaim path of `BytesMut::reserve`, the condition
```rs
if v_capacity >= new_cap + offset
```
uses an unchecked addition. When `new_cap + offset` overflows `usize` in release builds, this condition may incorrectly pass, causing `self.cap` to be set to a value that exceeds the actual allocated capacity. Subsequent APIs such as `spare_capacity_mut()` then trust this corrupted `cap` value and may create out-of-bounds slices, leading to UB.

This behavior is observable in release builds (integer overflow wraps), whereas de

expect.note: Overflow needs BytesMut::reserve(additional) with additional near usize::MAX (new_cap+offset wrapping). All reserve calls on the request path use bounded sizes (actix-http h1/dispatcher.rs:989 HW_BUFFER_SIZE, h1/mod.rs:61, encoder.rs:170/269/301/438, helpers.rs fixed 50); meilisearch/src has no BytesMut reserve. No attacker-sized reserve found.

Default plain bind (main.rs:184 -> HttpService::tcp, HTTP/1 only) does not reach it. facts.advisory_summary:
Rustls: TLS 1.3 handshake messages incorrectly accepted across encryption level boundaries — Rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level when they followed a key-changing message in the same record. The handshake transcript is still authenticated, so a network-position attacker cannot use this to alter or complete a handshake; the practical effect is that a peer could send handshake messages that should be encrypted in plaintext without rustls rejecting the connection.

This issue affects rustls versions 0.23.13 through 0.23.44 inclusive.

# Original report
##

expect.note: rustls 0.23.20 is in the affected range 0.23.13-0.23.44. Native TLS server too when MEILI_SSL_CERT_PATH/KEY are set (option.rs:647-685, main.rs:182). The flawed TLS 1.3 handshake message handling runs on peer data (remote server / network attacker on outbound paths). Practical impact is minimal because the transcript is still authenticated.

facts.advisory_summary:
tar has a PAX header desynchronization issue — ### Summary

When a tar stream contains multiple "header" entries prior to a file entry, tar-rs applies the PAX header (`x`) to the _next_ entry in the stream, regardless of type. tar-rs `unpack_in` can chmod arbitrary directories by following symlinks — ## Summary

When unpacking a tar archive, the `tar` crate's `unpack_dir` function uses `fs::metadata()` to check whether a path that already exists is a directory. Because `fs::metadata()` follows symbolic links, a crafted tarball containing a symlink entry followed by a directory entry with the same name causes the crate to treat the symlink target as a valid existing directory — and subsequently apply `chmod` to it. This allows an attacker to modify the permissions of arbitrary directories outside the extraction root.
